claim: Spiking activity of Purkinje cells differs between cerebellar modules and correlates with their expression of the glycolytic enzyme aldolase C or zebrin.
source: In this study, we show in awake mice at rest that spiking activity of Purkinje cells, the sole output cells of the cerebellar cortex, differs between cerebellar modules and correlates with their expression of the glycolytic enzyme aldolase C or zebrin.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented throughout the manuscript showing differences in firing frequencies between zebrin-positive and zebrin-negative Purkinje cells.

claim: Simple spike and complex spike frequencies were significantly higher in Purkinje cells located in zebrin-negative than zebrin-positive modules.
source: Simple spike and complex spike frequencies were significantly higher in Purkinje cells located in zebrin-negative than zebrin-positive modules.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental measurements presented in the abstract and detailed in the results section.

claim: The difference in simple spike frequency persisted when the synaptic input to, but not intrinsic activity of, Purkinje cells was manipulated.
source: The difference in simple spike frequency persisted when the synaptic input to, but not intrinsic activity of, Purkinje cells was manipulated.
evidence: This claim is supported by experiments using mutant mice and in vitro recordings with blocked synaptic inputs.

claim: Blocking TRPC3 attenuated the simple spike frequency difference between zebrin-positive and zebrin-negative modules.
source: Blocking TRPC3, the effector channel of a cascade of proteins that have zebrin-like distribution patterns, attenuated the simple spike frequency difference.
evidence: This claim is supported by pharmacological experiments using TRPC3 blockers both in vitro and in vivo.

claim: Zebrin-discriminated cerebellar modules operate at different frequencies, which depend on activation of TRPC3.
source: Our results indicate that zebrin-discriminated cerebellar modules operate at different frequencies, which depend on activation of TRPC3, and that this property is relevant for all cerebellar functions.
evidence: This claim is supported by the combined experimental data showing frequency differences and TRPC3 blocker effects.

claim: The cerebellum has a unique cyto-architecture characterized by the crystalline matrix of its sagittally oriented PC dendrites and climbing fibers and its orthogonally running parallel fibers.
source: The unique cyto-architecture of the cerebellum is characterized by the crystalline matrix of its sagittally oriented PC dendrites and climbing fibers and its orthogonally running parallel fibers (Larsell, 1972; Voogd, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature on cerebellar anatomy.

claim: The ubiquitous nature of the cerebellar cortex matrix made scientists predict in 1967 that this neuronal machine was probably the first to be elucidated.
source: The ubiquitous nature of this relatively simple matrix throughout all lobules and modules of the cerebellar cortex made scientists predict in 1967 that this neuronal machine was probably the first to be elucidated (Eccles, 1967).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Eccles, 1967.

claim: The amount of evidence for physiological differences within the cerebellar cortex is limited.
source: For example, the amount of evidence for physiological differences within the cerebellar cortex is limited and there is little comparative analysis of spiking activity throughout the cerebellar cortex in adult awake animals.
evidence: This claim is based on the authors' assessment of the existing literature.

claim: The cerebellum is still considered physiologically homogeneous.
source: In fact, even most slice physiology studies do not discriminate between lobules or modules, indicative of the fact that the cerebellum is still considered physiologically homogeneous.
evidence: This claim is based on the authors' assessment of common practices in cerebellar research.

claim: Zebrin is highly expressed by specific bands of Purkinje cells.
source: The best-known of these molecules are the zebrins, which are highly expressed by specific bands of Purkinje cells (PCs), that is the sole output of the cerebellar cortex.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about zebrin expression patterns.

claim: Immunostainings for both zebrin I and II give rise to symmetric stripes that are oriented perpendicular to the cerebellar folds.
source: Immunostainings for both zebrin I and II give rise to symmetric stripes that are oriented perpendicular to the cerebellar folds (Brochu et al., 1990; Leclerc et al., 1990).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies describing zebrin staining patterns.

claim: The combined presence of zebrin-positive and zebrin-negative PCs can be found in all vertebrate classes.
source: The combined presence of zebrin-positive and zebrin-negative PCs can be found in all vertebrate classes, and zebra-like patterns are present in the cerebellum of birds and mammals, varying from pigeons and mice up to monkeys and humans (Brochu et al., 1990; Sillitoe et al., 2003; Marzban and Hawkes, 2011; Graham and Wylie, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations documenting zebrin patterns across species.

claim: Adjacent PCs with zebrin II are located in the same bands, receive CF inputs from the same part of the inferior olive, and project their axons to the same part of the cerebellar nuclei.
source: In most cases, adjacent PCs with zebrin II (from hereon referred to as zebrin) are located in the same bands, receive CF inputs from the same part of the inferior olive, and project their axons to the same part of the cerebellar nuclei (Voogd and Ruigrok, 2004; Pijpers et al., 2006; Sugihara and Shinoda, 2007; Apps and Hawkes, 2009; Sugihara et al., 2009; Sugihara, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations describing the anatomical organization of zebrin-related modules.

claim: Individual mossy fibers often adhere to the same zebrin signature.
source: Moreover, although their various terminal rosettes may be located in different parts of the cerebellar cortex, individual mossy fibers often also adhere to the same zebrin signature (Pijpers et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Pijpers et al., 2006.

claim: Zebrin has been identified as the glycolytic enzyme aldolase C.
source: Since zebrin has been identified as the glycolytic enzyme aldolase C, its presence might in principle be linked to the level of metabolic and/or electrophysiological activity.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about the molecular identity of zebrin.

claim: The distribution of zebrin in the cerebellum is similar to that of the excitatory amino acid transporter 4 (EAAT4).
source: Indeed, the distribution of zebrin in the cerebellum is similar to that of the excitatory amino acid transporter 4 (EAAT4) and complementary to splice variant b of the metabotropic glutamate receptor 1 (mGluR1b) (Dehnes et al., 1998; Mateos et al., 2001; Wadiche and Jahr, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies describing the distribution patterns of these proteins.

claim: The distribution of zebrin in the cerebellum is complementary to splice variant b of the metabotropic glutamate receptor 1 (mGluR1b).
source: Indeed, the distribution of zebrin in the cerebellum is similar to that of the excitatory amino acid transporter 4 (EAAT4) and complementary to splice variant b of the metabotropic glutamate receptor 1 (mGluR1b) (Dehnes et al., 1998; Mateos et al., 2001; Wadiche and Jahr, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies describing the distribution patterns of these proteins.

claim: Several proteins in a molecular cascade linked to mGluR1 are expressed in zebrin-like bands, including the IP3-receptor, PLCβ3/4, PKCδ, and NCS-1.
source: Intracellularly, several proteins in a molecular cascade linked to mGluR1 are also expressed in zebrin-like bands, including the IP3-receptor (Furutama et al., 2010), PLCβ3/4 (Sarna et al., 2006), PKCδ (Barmack et al., 2000), and NCS-1 (Jinno et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to studies describing the expression patterns of these proteins.

claim: The molecular cascade linked to mGluR1 controls the activity of TRPC3.
source: This cascade controls the activity of the transient receptor potential cation channel type C3 (TRPC3) (Hartmann et al., 2008), which in turn can influence the firing activity of PCs (Sekerkova et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies describing the molecular cascade and TRPC3 function.

claim: TRPC3 can influence the firing activity of PCs.
source: This cascade controls the activity of the transient receptor potential cation channel type C3 (TRPC3) (Hartmann et al., 2008), which in turn can influence the firing activity of PCs (Sekerkova et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sekerkova et al., 2013.

claim: The SS firing frequency was significantly higher in Z− zones than in Z+ zones (Z−: 96.1 ± 15.4 Hz, Z+: 61.4 ± 19.3 Hz, t = 9.942, p<0.001).
source: The SS firing frequency was significantly higher in Z− zones than in Z+ zones (Z−: 96.1 ± 15.4 Hz, Z+: 61.4 ± 19.3 Hz, t = 9.942, p<0.001) (Figure 1H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in vivo recordings and statistical analysis shown in Figure 1H.

claim: The climbing fiber pause was significantly longer in Z+ zones than in Z− zones.
source: In line with this the climbing fiber pause was also significantly longer (t = −7.482, p<0.001) in Z+ zones (Figure 1I) (see also Paukert et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in vivo recordings and statistical analysis shown in Figure 1I.

claim: The waveform and regularity of SSs did not consistently depend on zebrin identity.
source: In contrast to the SS firing frequency and climbing fiber pause, the waveform and regularity of SSs did not consistently depend on zebrin identity in that average half-width and mean coefficient of variation for adjacent intervals (CV2) were not significantly different between Z− and Z+ PCs (half-width: t = −1.133, p=0.260, data not shown; CV2: t = 1.197, p=0.234) (Figure 1F–J).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing no significant differences in these parameters.

claim: The difference in simple spike firing frequency between Z+ and Z− Purkinje cells is linked to zebrin identity, rather than lobular location.
source: The difference in simple spike firing frequency was pertained in this subset of Purkinje cell recordings (Z+: 36.0 ± 15.5 Hz; Z−: 75.8 ± 19.5 Hz; t = 4.618, p<0.001), indicating that this difference is linked to zebrin identity, rather than lobular location.
evidence: This claim is supported by experiments using EAAT4-eGFP mice to record from adjacent zebrin-positive and zebrin-negative bands.

claim: The difference in simple spike activity between Z+ and Z− PCs is consistently present throughout all transverse zones.
source: We consistently observed a similar difference in simple spike activity between Z+ and Z− PCs in each zone, independent of the location within the cerebellar cortex (Figure 2D–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from recordings across different transverse zones shown in Figure 2D-E.

claim: Z+ PCs firing rate is lower in the anterior zone when compared to the nodular zone.
source: Whereas the simple spike firing frequency of Z− PCs is comparable over different transverse zones, Z+ PCs firing rate is lower in the anterior zone when compared to the nodular zone (p=0.018, One-way ANOVA followed by Tukey's post-hoc test).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data comparing Z+ PCs across transverse zones.

claim: There is a gradual increase in zebrin-positive modules from lobule I to lobule X in the vermis and the corresponding lobules in the hemispheres.
source: If the SS activity of PCs depends on the presence of zebrin, one should also observe differences between lobules, as there is a gradual increase in zebrin-positive modules and, thus, average zebrin intensity from lobule I to lobule X in the vermis and the corresponding lobules in the hemispheres (Sugihara and Shinoda, 2004) (Figure 1G, Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sugihara and Shinoda, 2004, and illustrated in figures.

claim: The firing frequency and climbing fiber pause of SS activity show robust and consistent correlations with the averaged intensity of zebrin staining.
source: Both the firing frequency and climbing fiber pause of SS activity, among the different lobules in the vermis and the hemispheres, show robust and consistent correlations with the averaged intensity of zebrin staining (for firing frequency, vermis: r = 0.893, p=0.007; hemisphere: r = 1.000, p<0.001; for climbing fiber pause, vermis: r = −0.929, p=0.003; hemisphere: r = −1.000, p<0.001) (Figure 3A–C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The CV2 of SSs could not be consistently related to the zebrin intensity in the vermis and hemispheres.
source: In contrast, the CV2 of SSs could not be consistently related to the zebrin intensity in the vermis and hemispheres (vermis: r = 0.929, p=0.003; hemisphere: r = −0.300, p=0.624) (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis showing inconsistent relationships across brain regions.

claim: Reduced tonic SS activity of PCs at rest in Z+ modules will lead to enhanced activity of the GABAergic neurons in the cerebellar nuclei that inhibit inferior olivary neurons.
source: Reduced tonic SS activity of PCs at rest, as observed in Z+ modules, will lead to enhanced activity of the GABAergic neurons in the cerebellar nuclei that inhibit inferior olivary neurons (Chen et al., 2010; De Zeeuw et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from known circuit connectivity supported by citations.

claim: The CS activity of immunostaining identified Z+ PCs was significantly lower than that in Z− PCs (Z−: 1.13 ± 0.25 Hz, Z+: 0.92 ± 0.28 Hz, t = 3.926, p<0.001).
source: The CS activity of immunostaining identified Z+ PCs was significantly lower than that in Z− PCs (same PCs as described in Figure 1G–J; Z−: 1.13 ± 0.25 Hz, Z+: 0.92 ± 0.28 Hz, t = 3.926, p<0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in vivo recordings and statistical analysis.

claim: Climbing fibers evoked prolonged EPSCs in Z+ Purkinje cells.
source: Since climbing fibers evoked prolonged EPSCs in Z+ Purkinje cells (Paukert et al., 2010), we also investigated the half-width of the first upward deflection in potential and the integrated deviation of the CS potential from zero.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Paukert et al., 2010.

claim: Both half-width and spike area of complex spikes were significantly higher in immunostaining identified Z+ PCs.
source: Both parameters were significantly higher in immunostaining identified Z+ PCs (half-width: t = −3.269, p=0.001, spike area: t = −2.523, p=0.013) (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Four different types of SS responses following the climbing fiber pause can be distinguished: normal, facilitation, suppression, and oscillation.
source: Based on the peri-CS time histograms, we could distinguish four different types of SS responses following the climbing fiber pause. These included a neutral pattern (i.e., normal type), a pattern with increased SS activity (i.e., facilitation type), and two patterns with decreased SS activity, one without and one with a superimposed oscillatory effect (i.e., suppression and oscillation type, respectively) (Figure 4E).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of peri-CS time histograms shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The facilitation type of cells prevail in the Z− zones, whereas the suppression and oscillation type of cells occur predominantly in the Z+ zones.
source: Even though the normal type dominated in both Z− and Z+ PCs, the suppression and oscillation types only occurred in Z+ PCs. The facilitation type occurred in both Z− and Z+ PCs, but significantly more in the Z− areas (Z−: 17 /47, Z+: 6/57; χ2 = 9.835, p=0.002, Pearson's Chi-squared test) (Figure 4F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The oscillation type showed a combination of low SS frequency and low CV.
source: Attempts to find other parameters correlating with the response type were largely unsuccessful, except for the oscillation type, which showed a combination of low SS frequency and low CV (Figure 4G).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: The average SS firing frequency was, on average, 22 ± 7% lower over all lobules in vitro than that in vivo.
source: The average SS firing frequency was, on average, 22 ± 7% lower over all lobules in vitro than that in vivo indicating that the larger part of SS activity is internally driven by PCs.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of in vitro and in vivo experimental data.

claim: The differential firing frequency pattern over all lobules in vitro correlated with that in vivo (r = 0.916, p=0.010).
source: The dominant impact of intrinsic PC activity was also reflected by the finding that the differential firing frequency pattern over all lobules in vitro correlated with that in vivo (r = 0.916, p=0.010, Pearson's correlation) (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis of in vitro and in vivo data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The in vitro SS firing frequency of PCs in lobules III was significantly higher than that in lobule X.
source: For example, the in vitro SS firing frequency of PCs in lobules III, which are predominantly Z−, was alike the in vivo recordings significantly higher than that in lobule X, where PCs are Z+ (t = 2.844, p=0.007).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in vitro recordings and statistical analysis.

claim: The higher firing frequency in lobule III was associated with a higher intrinsic excitability in lobule III compared to lobule X.
source: This higher firing frequency in lobule III was associated with a higher intrinsic excitability in lobule III compared to lobule X, reinforcing the interpretation that the difference is predominantly intrinsic to Purkinje cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1) (see also Kim et al., 2012a).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data on intrinsic excitability shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and a citation.

claim: In both a6-Cacna1a and PC-Δγ2 mutant mice the differences in vivo in SS firing frequency between lobules I–III and lobule X were still significant.
source: In both a6-Cacna1a and PC-Δγ2 mutant mice the differences in vivo in SS firing frequency between lobules I–III and lobule X were still significant, analogous to that in normal mice (a6-Cacna1a, I-III: 75.1 ± 19.0 Hz, X: 50.2 ± 10.2 Hz, t = 3.979, p<0.001; PC-Δγ2, I-III: 89.8 ± 14.9 Hz, X: 60.9 ± 15.6 Hz, t = 4.876, p<0.001) (Figure 5E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from mutant mice shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The CV2 values of SS activity were significantly reduced not only in vitro, but also in vivo in both a6-Cacna1a and PC-Δγ2 mutants as compared to wild-types.
source: In contrast, the CV2 values of SS activity were significantly reduced not only in vitro, but also in vivo in both a6-Cacna1a and PC-Δγ2 mutants as compared to wild-types (Figure 5F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from mutant mice shown in Figure 5F.

claim: The SS firing frequency is largely determined by intrinsic properties of PCs, whereas the level of regularity appears to be predominantly determined by external inputs.
source: Together, these data suggest that the SS firing frequency is largely determined by intrinsic properties of PCs, whereas the level of regularity appears to be predominantly determined by external inputs.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the combined experimental data from in vitro recordings and mutant mice.

claim: When the products of aldolase C (GAP and DHAP) were introduced to the ACSF in in vitro recordings, SS firing increased in both lobule III and lobule X.
source: In fact, when the products of aldolase C, that is glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate (GAP) and dihydroxyacetone phosphate (DHAP), were introduced to the ACSF in our in vitro recordings, SS firing increased in both the largely zebrin-negative lobule III and zebrin-positive lobule X (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), arguing against the possibility that aldolase C's enzymatic function directly contributes to a lower SS firing frequency in Z+ PCs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Both TRPC3 blockers (genistein and Pyr3) had a significant impact on PC activity reducing the firing frequency in lobule III without a significant effect in lobule X.
source: Both TRPC3 blockers had a significant impact on PC activity reducing the firing frequency in lobule III (genistein, p<0.001; Pyr3, p<0.001 vs vehicle control, one-way followed by Tukey's post-hoc test) without a significant effect in lobule X (p=0.271 and p=1.000 vs vehicle respectively, one-way ANOVA followed by Tukey's post-hoc test) (Figure 6A,B)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in vitro recordings with TRPC3 blockers shown in Figure 6A,B.

claim: Wash-in of Pyr3 had a robust effect on SS firing frequency of PCs in lobule III and this effect was significantly larger than that in lobule X.
source: Wash-in of Pyr3 had a robust effect on SS firing frequency of PCs in lobule III (pre: 49.9 ± 7.9 Hz; post: 25.5 ± 9.9 Hz; t = 5.412, p=0.002, paired Student's t test) and this effect was significantly larger than that in lobule X (reduction, lobule III: 48.2 ± 19.7%; lobule X: 8.5 ± 16.6%; t = 4.069, p=0.002) (Figure 6D,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from wash-in experiments shown in Figure 6D,E.

claim: Blocking EAAT4 in vitro had no significant effect on the activity of Purkinje cells in either lobule III or lobule X.
source: Based on the higher expression of EAAT4 in Z+ Purkinje cells, blocking EAAT4 would arguably affect lobule X more than lobule III, but the general EAAT blocker DL-TBOA had no significant effect on the activity of Purkinje cells in either lobule (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A,B) (lobule III: t = 1.219, p=0.227; lobule X: t = −0.597, p=0.533)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in vitro recordings with EAAT4 blocker shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: In vivo, both genistein and Pyr3 caused a decrease in SS activity in lobules I–III, while no significant effect was recorded in lobule X.
source: In line with the in vitro data, both genistein and Pyr3 (i.p. and i.c.v., 240 mg/kg and 200 µg, respectively) caused a decrease in SS activity in lobules I–III, lasting for several hours (vehicle: 90.6 ± 13.3 Hz; genistein: 74.6 ± 14.9 Hz; Pyr3: 61.6 ± 15.5 Hz; both p<0.001 vs vehicle, One-way ANOVA followed by Tukey's post-hoc test), while no significant effect was recorded in lobule X (vehicle: 52.9 ± 13.3 Hz; genistein: 57.5 ± 20.8 Hz,; Pyr3: 51.1 ± 14.3 Hz, p=0.546 and p=0.887 vs vehicle, One-way ANOVA followed by Tukey's post-hoc test) (Figure 6F,G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in vivo recordings with TRPC3 blockers shown in Figure 6F,G.

claim: TRPC3 contributes to the elevated SS activity in zebrin-negative PC zones.
source: Together, these data suggest that TRPC3 contributes to the elevated SS activity in zebrin-negative PC zones.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the combined experimental data with TRPC3 blockers.

claim: This study provides the first evidence for ubiquitously organized differences in cerebellar Purkinje cell firing activity in vivo.
source: This study provides, to our knowledge, the first evidence for ubiquitously organized differences in cerebellar Purkinje cell firing activity in vivo and for the correlation of these differences to a marker protein, zebrin II.
evidence: This claim is based on the authors' assessment of their findings in the context of existing literature.

claim: Purkinje cells within the same module operate around a preferred range of intrinsically determined SS firing frequencies.
source: As zebrin, as a biomarker, can be associated with the modular organization of the olivo-cortico-nuclear circuit (Brochu et al., 1990; Voogd et al., 2003; Pijpers et al., 2006; Sugihara and Shinoda, 2007), our results indicate that Purkinje cells within the same module operate around a preferred range of intrinsically determined SS firing frequencies and that this activity is different from modules with a different zebrin identity.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data and citations about modular organization.

claim: CS activity is altered as a secondary effect of differences in SS activity.
source: Moreover, presumably as a secondary effect, CS activity is also altered.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing correlated changes in CS activity.

claim: The difference in SS firing frequency is probably largely determined by the intrinsic properties of PCs.
source: The difference in SS firing frequency is probably largely determined by the intrinsic properties of PCs, as this difference was maintained in the reduced slice preparation, in which the inputs are blocked, as well as in mouse mutants, in which the excitatory (a6-Cacna1a mice) or inhibitory (PC-Δγ2 mice) inputs are attenuated.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data in reduced preparations and mutant mice.

claim: The level of regularity of firing (CV2) was not consistently dependent on zebrin identity, but significantly altered by impairing the excitatory and/or inhibitory inputs.
source: In contrast, the level of regularity of firing (i.e., CV2) was not consistently dependent on zebrin identity, but significantly altered by impairing the excitatory and/or inhibitory inputs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from mutant mice and in vitro recordings.

claim: Reduction of simple spike frequency in lobule III in vivo for several minutes to hours by Pyr3 application also reduced complex spike frequency.
source: In fact, reduction of simple spike frequency in lobule III in vivo for several minutes to hours by Pyr3 application also reduced complex spike frequency, supporting the indirect control of simple spikes on complex spike activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in vivo recordings with Pyr3 application.

claim: Temporary increases in climbing fiber-evoked CS activity suppress SS frequency providing a homeostatic control mechanism within an olivocerebellar module.
source: Interestingly, temporary increases in climbing fiber-evoked CS activity suppress SS frequency providing a homeostatic control mechanism within an olivocerebellar module (Mathews et al., 2012; Coddington et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies describing homeostatic mechanisms.

claim: External inputs to PCs may control the precise temporal coding of SS activity at rest as well as the firing frequency and dynamic range during natural sensory stimulation.
source: Thus, whereas the external inputs to PCs may control the precise temporal coding of SS activity at rest as well as the firing frequency and dynamic range during natural sensory stimulation (Badura et al., 2013; Galliano et al., 2013), their intrinsic properties appear to determine the baseline frequencies of SSs as well as CSs at rest, around which they can operate.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data and citations.

claim: Intrinsic properties of PCs appear to determine the baseline frequencies of SSs as well as CSs at rest.
source: Thus, whereas the external inputs to PCs may control the precise temporal coding of SS activity at rest as well as the firing frequency and dynamic range during natural sensory stimulation (Badura et al., 2013; Galliano et al., 2013), their intrinsic properties appear to determine the baseline frequencies of SSs as well as CSs at rest, around which they can operate.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data.

claim: TRPC3 gene expression appears to vary from anterior to posterior with higher levels in the anterior, largely zebrin-negative, lobules.
source: It should be noted that, although TRPC3 gene expression appears to vary from anterior to posterior with higher levels in the anterior, largely zebrin-negative, lobules (Allen Brain Atlas, www.brain-map.org), there is no immunohistochemical evidence for differences in protein levels (Hartmann and et al, 2008; Becker et al., 2009; Sekerkova et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to the Allen Brain Atlas and citations.

claim: There is no immunohistochemical evidence for differences in TRPC3 protein levels across the cerebellum.
source: It should be noted that, although TRPC3 gene expression appears to vary from anterior to posterior with higher levels in the anterior, largely zebrin-negative, lobules (Allen Brain Atlas, www.brain-map.org), there is no immunohistochemical evidence for differences in protein levels (Hartmann and et al, 2008; Becker et al., 2009; Sekerkova et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies examining TRPC3 protein expression.

claim: The differential effect of blocking TRPC3 suggests that its activity might be higher in Z− PCs.
source: If the expression of TRPC3 is indeed homogeneous throughout the cerebellum, the differential effect of blocking TRPC3 suggests that its activity might be higher in Z− PCs.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data with TRPC3 blockers.

claim: Zebrin II or aldolase C bears the capacity to bind IP3.
source: In fact, zebrin II or aldolase C, which is not likely to be involved via its enzymatic function, bears the capacity to bind IP3 (Baron et al., 1999), and thus could potentially reduce the activation of TRPC3 in Z+ PCs, through the IP3-receptor.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Baron et al., 1999.

claim: mGluR1 can be tonically activated.
source: At the same time, mGluR1 subtype b is expressed in a pattern complementary to that of zebrin (Mateos et al., 2001), and it has been shown that mGluR1 can be tonically activated, that mGlurR1 blockers can reduce SS firing frequency (Yamakawa and Hirano, 1999; Coesmans et al., 2003; Chanda and Xu-Friedman, 2011), and that mGluR1-evoked depolarizing currents can be blocked with TRPC3-selective blockers (Kiyonaka et al., 2009; Kim et al., 2012b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies describing mGluR1 function.

claim: mGluR1 blockers can reduce SS firing frequency.
source: At the same time, mGluR1 subtype b is expressed in a pattern complementary to that of zebrin (Mateos et al., 2001), and it has been shown that mGluR1 can be tonically activated, that mGlurR1 blockers can reduce SS firing frequency (Yamakawa and Hirano, 1999; Coesmans et al., 2003; Chanda and Xu-Friedman, 2011), and that mGluR1-evoked depolarizing currents can be blocked with TRPC3-selective blockers (Kiyonaka et al., 2009; Kim et al., 2012b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies describing mGluR1 blocker effects.

claim: mGluR1-evoked depolarizing currents can be blocked with TRPC3-selective blockers.
source: At the same time, mGluR1 subtype b is expressed in a pattern complementary to that of zebrin (Mateos et al., 2001), and it has been shown that mGluR1 can be tonically activated, that mGlurR1 blockers can reduce SS firing frequency (Yamakawa and Hirano, 1999; Coesmans et al., 2003; Chanda and Xu-Friedman, 2011), and that mGluR1-evoked depolarizing currents can be blocked with TRPC3-selective blockers (Kiyonaka et al., 2009; Kim et al., 2012b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies describing TRPC3 blocker effects on mGluR1-evoked currents.

claim: The low and high baseline frequencies of zebrin-positive and zebrin-negative PCs appear to be in line with their propensities for induction of long-term potentiation (LTP) and long-term depression (LTD), respectively.
source: Interestingly, the low and high baseline frequencies of zebrin-positive and zebrin-negative PCs also appear to be in line with their propensities for induction of long-term potentiation (LTP) and long-term depression (LTD), respectively (Wadiche and Jahr, 2005; Wang et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data and citations about plasticity mechanisms.

claim: Entrainment of cerebellar nuclei neurons by synchronized SS input from PCs may occur at 50–80 Hz, but is impaired at 100 Hz.
source: Likewise, entrainment of cerebellar nuclei neurons by synchronized SS input from PCs, which results in phase-locking of connected neurons, may occur at 50–80 Hz, but is impaired at 100 Hz (Person and Raman, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Person and Raman, 2012.

claim: The cerebellar nuclei can be divided based on the zebrin expression pattern, with a rostral half that receives, predominantly, input from zebrin-negative PC's and a caudal part that mostly receives zebrin-positive inputs.
source: The cerebellar nuclei can also be divided based on the zebrin expression pattern, with a rostral half that receives, predominantly, input from zebrin-negative PC's and a caudal part that mostly receives zebrin-positive inputs (Sugihara and Shinoda, 2007; Sugihara et al., 2009; Sugihara, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies describing the organization of cerebellar nuclei.

claim: PC input to cerebellar nuclei neurons may be segregated on the basis of frequency.
source: This implies that PC input to cerebellar nuclei neurons may be segregated on the basis of frequency, and that as a consequence the output of cerebellar nuclei neurons located within zebrin-positive and zebrin-negative territories may be distinctly different.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data and anatomical organization.

claim: Purkinje cells were identified by the presence of SSs and CSs and the consistent presence of a pause in SS firing after a CS (climbing fiber pause).
source: Purkinje cells were identified by the presence of SSs and CSs and the consistent presence of a pause in SS firing after a CS (i.e., climbing fiber pause) (Figure 1C–F).
evidence: This describes the methodological criteria used to identify Purkinje cells in recordings.

claim: Of the 104 PCs included in the analysis, 47 and 57 cells were located in Z− and Z+ zones, respectively.
source: Of the 104 PCs included in the analysis (50 mice), 47 and 57 cells were located in Z− and Z+ zones, respectively (Figure 1G, plot adapted from Sugihara and Quy, 2007).
evidence: This describes the sample size and distribution of recorded cells.
